student.question: Who is the service owner of the decision on closed tickets and reopening?
student.answer: The service owner of the decision on closed tickets and reopening is The Incident Manager, process owner of incident management. Source: [DECISIONS.md]
student.context:
[DECISIONS.md]
Decisions > C2 - Closed tickets and reopening
**Decision:** A closed ticket is immutable. Reopen works from resolved only, within 7 days of resolved_at; a
reopen request on a closed ticket answers 409 whatever its age, and further work on the same issue is a new
ticket that references the closed one via related_to. The minimal conflicting part of R-10, the words "or
closed" and "or closure", is rejected; reopening a resolved ticket, the rest of R-10, stands together with all
of R-09.

**Rejected alternative:** Reopen allowed from closed as well, within 7 days of closed_at, with the record
becoming immutable only after that window.

[DECISIONS.md]
Decisions > C2 - Closed tickets and reopening
**Reason:** Closure is the point where the record becomes evidence: it feeds SLA attainment reports, problem
records and the monthly service review, and a record that can silently change after that point makes every
report reproducible only by luck. The 7-day reopen window after resolution already gives the reporter the "the
fix did not work" path that R-10 is for; the resolved state exists precisely so that closure can wait until
the reporter has confirmed. A new ticket linked via related_to preserves the history of both records and gives
problem management a countable signal, how many closed tickets spawned follow-up work, instead of a mutated
one.

**Service owner:** The Incident Manager, process owner of incident management, who signs off the closure rules
because closure is what makes the incident record trustworthy for reporting and problem management.

**Customer outcome:** A reporter whose fix failed within a week reopens the resolved ticket without friction;
once the ticket is closed, the customer raises a linked ticket and the history of both is preserved, so the
reports the customer relies on (SLA attainment, recurring issues) stay true.

[specs/spec.md]
Feature specification: svcdesk, the service-desk API > Functional requirements
  `paused` evaluated at the request's `now`; equality is not a breach; a reopened ticket is unresolved again
  and keeps its resolution target (R-15, R-16).
- FR-5 State machine (R-07, R-08): ack from new, start from acknowledged, resolve from in_progress, close from
  resolved, reopen from resolved within 7 days of `resolved_at` and, under C2 = reopen only, from closed within
  7 days of `closed_at` (R-09, R-10, R-11). Everything else is 409 with an `error` object; unknown ids are 404.
- FR-6 `GET /tickets` returns every matching ticket in one array, optionally filtered by `state` and
  `priority`, without pagination (R-19); `GET /tickets/{id}` returns one ticket or 404 (R-18).
- FR-7 `GET /health` returns `{"status": "ok", "service": "svcdesk", ...}`; unknown paths are 404 with a JSON
  body (R-02, R-25).
- FR-8 Test clock (R-21): with `SVCDESK_TEST_CLOCK=1` every request may carry `X-Test-Clock`; a header that

[specs/spec.md]
Feature specification: svcdesk, the service-desk API > User stories
1. As a reporter I raise a ticket with a title, a description, my name, and the impact and urgency of the
   incident, and I get back a ticket with an id, a computed priority and two SLA deadlines.
2. As a desk agent I move a ticket through acknowledged, in progress, resolved and closed, and the service
   records when each step happened.
3. As a reporter whose fix did not work I reopen a resolved ticket within seven days (and a closed one, if the
   desk's policy allows it) and the ticket goes back to in progress.
4. As a service level manager I ask at any instant whether a ticket's acknowledgement or resolution target is
   breached and whether its clock is currently paused.
5. As the checker I drive the service with a per-request test clock so that every scenario is reproducible.

**Decision:** P1 acknowledgement (15 min) and resolution (4 h) run on the wall clock, around the clock; P2 to

student.question: By how much were the clock-skewed commits later than the deployment that shipped them?
student.answer: The clock-skewed commits were later than the deployment by between 30 seconds and 15 minutes. Source: [EDGE-CASES.md]
student.context:
[EDGE-CASES.md]
Edge cases in the practice event log > E1 - clock skew produces a negative lead time
- What the log contains: three commits whose `at` is later than the deployment that shipped them, by between
  thirty seconds and fifteen minutes. Two machines disagreed about the time, which is the ordinary cause.
- What a default definition would have done: `max(0, ...)` is rare; dropping the pair is common, and so is
  reporting a negative median. Dropping is the dangerous one, because it is silent.
- Why the rule is defensible: a clamped pair keeps the deployment in the denominator, so the median is not
  biased upward by discarding exactly the fastest-looking observations, and the anomaly count makes the
  measurement problem visible instead of hiding it inside a metric nobody questions.

[EDGE-CASES.md]
Edge cases in the practice event log > E4 - a deployment with zero linked commits
- What the log contains: four production deployments whose `commits` list is empty - a configuration rollout,
  a re-run of a failed job, and the two the failure injections produced.
- What a default definition would have done: drop the deployment (which understates deployment frequency and
  the change fail rate denominator) or divide by zero computing its lead time.
- Why the rule is defensible: a deployment happened, so deployment frequency must count it, and if it failed,
  the change fail rate must count it too. What it cannot do is contribute a lead time, because there is no
  commit to measure from. The two facts live in different metrics and the rule keeps them apart.

[EDGE-CASES.md]
Edge cases in the practice event log > E2 - a revert of a revert
- What the log contains: two chains where a commit reverts a commit that is itself a revert. Under R-06 both
  revert commits inherit the original change, so three commits are one change.
- What a default definition would have done: count commits, not changes, and report three changes where there
  is one; or treat every revert as evidence of a failed change and inflate the rework rate.
- Why the rule is defensible: the unit DORA measures is a change that reaches users, and reverting a revert
  puts the original change back. Counting the round trip as three changes would reward churn, which is
  precisely the behaviour the instability metrics exist to detect.

student.question: What is the availability error budget of the /kb/search SLO in minutes?
student.answer: The availability error budget of the /kb/search SLO is 201.6 minutes. Source: [slo.md]
student.context:
[slo.md]
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Availability
**SLI**: the share of `/kb/search` requests answered without a 5xx. **SLO**: 99.5 % over 28 days.
**Error budget**: 0.5 % of requests, which at a steady rate is 201.6 minutes of total outage in the window.

The dependency itself fails about 0.16 % of the time (measured: 4 errors in 2,400 requests, and the profile's own
rate); a 99.9 % objective would leave a budget of 0.1 % that `kb-index` alone overspends every day, so every alert on
it would page for a failure nobody on this team can fix. 99.5 % leaves the dependency's normal failures at a burn
rate of about 0.3 and still pages when a real incident multiplies them.

[slo.md]
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Latency
**SLI**: the share of `/kb/search` requests answered within 0.3 s, counted from the histogram's `le="0.3"` bucket -
a boundary of the ladder, so the SLI is a count, not an interpolation. **SLO**: 99 % over 28 days.
**Error budget**: 1 % of requests, 403.2 minutes.

Measured with the published command, the p99 is about 236 ms and the p99.9 about 265 ms: the slow requests are a
narrow mode near 230 ms (about 3 % of requests), not a long tail. A threshold at the p99 would spend the whole budget
on the dependency's normal behaviour; 0.3 s sits above that mode, so a healthy service burns well under 1 % and the
budget is spent only when the slow mode moves or grows.

[slo.md]
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > front matter

  service: svcdesk
  route: /kb/search
  window: 28d
  slis:
    availability:
      objective: 0.995
      good: 'sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="svcdesk", http_route="/kb/search", http_response_status_code!~"5.."}[5m]))'
      valid: 'sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="svcdesk", http_route="/kb/search"}[5m]))'
      error_budget: {fraction: 0.005, minutes: 201.6}
    latency:
      objective: 0.99
      threshold_seconds: 0.3
      good: 'sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="svcdesk", http_route="/kb/search", le="0.3"}[5m]))'
      valid: 'sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="svcdesk", http_route="/kb/search"}[5m]))'
      error_budget: {fraction: 0.01, minutes: 403.2}
  alerts:
    - {alert: KbSearchLatencyBurnFast, sli: latency, burn_rate: 14.4, long_window: 1h, short_window: 5m}
    - {alert: KbSearchLatencyBurnSlow, sli: latency, burn_rate: 6, long_window: 6h, short_window: 30m}

student.question: How many boundaries does the latency histogram's bucket ladder have?
student.answer: The latency histogram's bucket ladder has 23 boundaries. Source: [slo.md]
student.context:
[slo.md]
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Buckets
The ladder (`src/svcdesk/metrics.py`) is coarse below 150 ms, a boundary every 10 ms from 180 ms to 280 ms, and 0.3 s
exact for the SLI: 23 boundaries. At q = 236 ms the containing bucket is (0.23, 0.24], 4 % of q; the checker's q
differs from a laptop's by a few per cent, which the 10 ms steps absorb on either side.

[slo.md]
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Latency
**SLI**: the share of `/kb/search` requests answered within 0.3 s, counted from the histogram's `le="0.3"` bucket -

Measured with the published command, the p99 is about 236 ms and the p99.9 about 265 ms: the slow requests are a
narrow mode near 230 ms (about 3 % of requests), not a long tail. A threshold at the p99 would spend the whole budget
on the dependency's normal behaviour; 0.3 s sits above that mode, so a healthy service burns well under 1 % and the
budget is spent only when the slow mode moves or grows.

[EVIDENCE.md]
Lab 7 evidence > Model
**Keys.** `events_by_actor` is `PRIMARY KEY ((actor, day, bucket), created_at, event_id)`: the `WHERE` names every
partition-key column - `actor` and `day` with `=`, `bucket` with `IN` over all B values - so the coordinator knows
exactly which B partitions to read, and `created_at` is the first clustering column, so the half-open window
`[from_ts, to_ts)` is a slice of each partition's sorted rows: no `ALLOW FILTERING`. `event_id` is the last
clustering column because many events share a second (21 of the bot's in the first two seconds of the slice), and
without it they would overwrite each other. `events_by_repo` is the same with `repo` in place of `actor`.
`events_by_ticket` is `PRIMARY KEY ((ticket_id), at, phase)`: one partition per ticket; `at` alone is not unique,
because my `svcdesk` stamps `created`, `acknowledged` and `resolved` with the same second when they come quickly
(my own ticket did: three events, all at 22:57:01), so `phase` is in the key too. `ticket_id` is `text`: my ids are
UUID strings, and `text` takes any id the stream sends.

student.question: How much did the recommendation service's container memory move during the incident?
student.answer: The recommendation service's container memory moved from 53.5 MB to 57.1 MB during the incident. Source: [postmortem.md]
student.context:
[postmortem.md]
Postmortem: the product catalogue failed and stalled, and pages took 15 seconds, for nine minutes > Impact
- **Slow pages and orders**: the p95 over five minutes of product-catalog, recommendation and the frontend reached
  15,000 ms, the top bucket, from 07:58 to 08:04 (23 ms, 7 ms and 46 ms on the healthy shop at 07:50:26);
  checkout's p95 reached 12,250 ms at 08:04 (91 ms healthy). Two orders took more than 5 s
  (`calls_total - duration_milliseconds_bucket{le="5000"}` of PlaceOrder, 0 at 07:55, 2 at 08:06).
- **Recommendations without cache**: recommendation's container memory moved only from 53.5 MB to 57.1 MB
  (`container_memory_usage_total_bytes{container_name="recommendation"}`, 07:55 to 08:06); its latency was already
  at the ceiling because of the stalled catalogue, so the cache failure's own share cannot be told apart in nine
  minutes.

[postmortem.md]
Postmortem: the product catalogue failed and stalled, and pages took 15 seconds, for nine minutes > Root Causes
Three flags of the shop's flag provider switched to failing values together. productCatalogFailure made
product-catalog answer GetProduct with an error for one product of the catalogue, so every order and every product
page holding that product failed. productCatalogLockContention made product-catalog's reads wait on a lock for up to
30 s, so every caller of the catalogue - the frontend's pages, recommendation's ListProducts, checkout's order
preparation - waited with it. recommendationCacheFailure disabled the recommendation service's cache, a resource
fault whose memory growth had barely started when it was switched off. What was already wrong: flags that can fail or
stall the one service every page depends on are switchable at runtime by a source that overrides the shop's own flag
file, with no change record and no alert that names them; and product-catalog is a single dependency of checkout,
the frontend and recommendation with no timeout shorter than its stall.

[postmortem.md]
Postmortem: the product catalogue failed and stalled, and pages took 15 seconds, for nine minutes > Summary
From 07:55:26 to 08:04:31 UTC three feature flags of the shop failed at once, all of them on the product catalogue's
path. Product-catalog's GetProduct failed for one product in ten, which failed 3 of 60 orders and 27 product pages;
product-catalog's reads stalled for up to 30 seconds at a time, which pushed the p95 of the frontend, of
recommendation and of product-catalog to the 15-second ceiling of the histogram and checkout's p95 to 12 seconds; and
the recommendation service ran without its cache. Switching the three flags off restored service nine minutes after
the onset.

student.question: What was the MTTA of the incident?
student.answer: The MTTA of the incident was 79 seconds. Source: [postmortem.md]
student.context:
[postmortem.md]
Postmortem: the product catalogue failed and stalled, and pages took 15 seconds, for nine minutes > What went wrong
The detecting alert was a P3 in a separate rule group, which fired a minute before any P1: the page waited for
checkout's error ratio to stay above 5 % for a minute, while the latency of every page was already at 15 s. The
recorded MTTA (79 s) is mostly that minute, not the on-call's reaction. The resource fault (recommendation cache)
left no signal any of the rules could separate from the catalogue stall.

[postmortem.md]
Postmortem: the product catalogue failed and stalled, and pages took 15 seconds, for nine minutes > Supporting information
`itsmlab incident 4` on the committed snapshot printed onset 07:55:26, detection 07:58:38 (ServiceLatencyRaised),
acknowledgement 07:59:57, recovery 08:05:38, MTTD 192 s, MTTA 79 s, MTTR 612 s. The pager's log shows seven
notifications: chat at 07:58:48 (ServiceLatencyRaised on product-catalog and recommendation) and 07:58:49
(FrontendLatencyHigh), before the P1 fired; pager firing at 07:59:49 (CheckoutErrorRate) and 08:01:49
(CheckoutLatencyHigh), resolved at 08:03:49 and 08:04:49; chat resolved at 08:05:48. The AI ledgers are
`ai-rca-eval.json` (qwen3:1.7b) and `ai-rca-eval-2.json` (qwen3:4b-instruct), compared in `ai-rca/COMPARISON.md`.
The rules are `prometheus/demo-alerts.yml`, the routes `alertmanager/alertmanager.yml`.

[EDGE-CASES.md]
Edge cases in the practice event log > E6 - overlapping incidents
- What the log contains: eleven pairs of incidents whose intervals intersect. Most of the overlap comes from
  the open incident of E5, whose interval runs to the end of the window and therefore meets every incident
  opened after it.
- What a default definition would have done: merge overlapping incidents into one, or add their durations up
  and call the total "downtime", double counting wall-clock that was only lived through once.
- Why the rule is defensible: recovery is a property of a deployment, not of an incident, so a failed
  deployment takes the resolution of its own covering incident and nothing is summed. E5 also shows why
  merging is the worse of the two errors: one incident nobody closed would swallow every other incident in
  the window and produce a single enormous "outage" that never happened.

student.question: How many failed searches did the hang cost in the flag run, and how many were predicted?
student.answer: The hang cost 84 failed searches in the flag run, and 88 were predicted. Source: [BLAST-RADIUS.md]
student.context:
[BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius > Blast radius
Without the shadow the same gate would pay at the 10 % step: errors at q = 0.6, c = 5, D = about 12 s (a scrape, a
look, the admin call): 5 + 40 x 0.1 x 0.6 x 12 = about 34; a hang (c = 0, q = 1) with D = 12 s of silence + up to 5 s
of scrape + 5 s of look = 22 s: 40 x 0.1 x 1 x 22 = 88. My flag runs measure that path, because a flag run has no
shadow: the hang above cost 84 against 88 predicted - D is the term that dominates: 15-16 s until my stall rule
(12 s without a new search, checked every 5 s) fires, up to 5 s of scrape before the last search shows, 2 s because
my looks read Prometheus 2 s in the past, and the admin call. The honest flag run's 8 candidate 5xx on 3,487 answers
(0.23 %) are kb-index's floor; the stable build's share (0.21 %) predicts 7 of them, so 1 counts. (My first flag practice run,
with the TEST builds, counted 10: its warm-up happened to have no 5xx, so its floor was 0.) What would push a run over
150: a first step of 25 % or more with the same D (40 x 0.25 x 1 x 22 = 220), a `[1m]` window that keeps the hang's old searches in view, or a gate that waits
for `min_requests` before it looks at arrivals at all.

[BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius > Blast radius
Beyond the four runs: `itsmlab verify 6 --seed p01` .. `p16` (run against the course's TEST builds of the images,
before the published ones reached my machine), every one with the gate of commit 29fa110, gave the
right outcome in all 64 canary runs (blast radius 0 for every bad candidate - all caught in the shadow - and 0 to 4
for the honest one) and all 32 flag runs (bad: 8 to 23 for errors and slow, 67 to 100 for the hang). Six of them
(p02, p03, p05, p07, p13, p14) again with the current gate (one read instant per look, below): the same 36
right outcomes, the hang's flag runs at 77 to 97. That spread is the case for the
shadow: 100 is two thirds of the ceiling, and it is what the hang costs at 10 % with a 12 s stall rule.

One bug the logs showed me: my counters were six separate queries, and when a scrape landed between the count and
its `le` bucket, a whole scrape's searches read as slow or as negative (the control's slow share once read -100 %).
Read at the start of a step, after the shadow's 200 searches a scrape, that could have rolled back the honest
candidate. Every look now reads all its counters at one instant 2 s in the past (commit e3fae3d).

[BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius > Blast radius
| run | behaviour | outcome | measured blast radius | c | w | q | D (s) | predicted |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `20261011T165046Z-rc.1` | hang (k = 40) | rolled back in the shadow, 28 s after the start: the canary's count stuck at 40 for 15 s while about 600 were mirrored | **0** | 0 | 0 (shadow) | 1 | about 20 | 0 |
| `20261011T165211Z-rc.2` | honest | promoted, 87 s: shadow (541 searches before the first user answer), 10 % for 45 s, 50 % for 20 s | **2** (4 candidate 5xx on 1,196 answers, floor 2) | - | 0.1, 0.5 | 0.0015 (kb-index) | - | about 0 |
| `20261011T165434Z-rc.3` | slow | rolled back in the shadow, 13 s: 36 of 111 searches over 0.3 s (32.4 %) against 10 % | **0** | 5 | 0 (shadow) | about 0.3 | about 8 | 0 |
| `20261011T165542Z-rc.4` | errors | rolled back in the shadow, 14 s: 77 of 182 searches 5xx (42.3 %) against 5 % | **0** | 5 | 0 (shadow) | about 0.42 | about 8 | 0 |
| `20261011T165652Z-rc.1` (flag) | hang (k = 40) | rolled back at flag 10 %, 37 s: no flag-on search for 15 s | **84** (all timeouts) | 0 | 0.10 | 1 | about 22 | 88 |

student.question: What did flagd's read-backs show at each step of the honest flag run?
student.answer: The flagd's read-backs showed 0/40, 4/40, 19/40, and 40/40 at each step of the honest flag run. Source: [BLAST-RADIUS.md]
student.context:
[BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius > Postmortem action
Commit 29fa110 implements the first half for every flag change my release process makes: each one goes through
`change_flag`, which writes it into the change record as a closed-loop action with its before and after ("flag
svcdesk-2-1: 10 % -> 50 % (step 2)"), and then reads the flag back from flagd itself - 40 OFREP evaluations with
random targeting keys - and records what flagd actually serves as a read-only action ("17 of 40 evaluations on").
A change flagd does not serve is a failed change: going dark fails the run before the candidate starts, and a step
that flagd does not apply rolls back. That matters because flagd silently ignores a flag file it cannot read; without
the read-back the record would claim a change that never happened - the opposite of what ITSM-103 wants. My practice
flag runs show it working: the honest flag run's record (`changes/20261011T165824Z-rc.2/CHANGE.md`) lists 0 -> 10 -> 50 -> 100 % with
read-backs of 0/40, 4/40, 19/40 and 40/40, and the hang's flag run records 0 -> 10 -> 0 % with each read back.

[BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius > Postmortem action
My Lab 4 postmortem (`postmortem.md`, my own: `baselines: {lab4: student}`) found that the incident was three
feature flags switched on together in the shop's flagd, with nobody recording the change: the on-call found them
only by reading `/flags.json` after the symptoms. Its action item **ITSM-103** (type prevent, owner platform team)
asks to "Record every runtime flag change as a change in svcdesk, and export the count of failing flags as a metric
the dashboards show". None of my five action items is a release-gate change in the strict sense - ITSM-101 and
ITSM-102 are alerting rules, ITSM-104 is a timeout in the shop's code, ITSM-105 a runbook step - and ITSM-103 is the
one a release process can honestly implement, because my `deploy.sh` itself changes a runtime flag (`svcdesk-2-1`,
Stretch 2).

[BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius > Change classification
- **start the candidate at weight 0 - closed-loop.** It changes nothing a user sees, and the procedure as a whole
  is pre-authorised; no person decides it per run.
- **read Prometheus, read the flag back from flagd - read-only.** They change nothing; they are the evidence.
- **set a weight or a flag share up a step - closed-loop.** The gate decides from its own readings that the last
  step passed. A person could not do better at 5 s intervals, and a `suggest` here would stall an unattended run.
- **roll back - closed-loop.** The cheapest, best-understood action: stable never stopped serving; one admin call.
- **promote - closed-loop**, and the one I would move to **approve-then-act** outside a course lab: in production
  the approval would be the standard-change model itself, signed by the service owner before the release window,
  and I would want a person to approve the promotion of a candidate that changes the data or the API.

What would change my classification: a false rollback of an honest candidate in practice (the procedure is not
well understood), or a bad candidate reaching users through the shadow (the bound does not hold).

student.question: About how many bytes per row did the instructor's hot partition take?
student.answer: The instructor's hot partition took about 66 bytes per row. Source: [EVIDENCE.md]
student.context:
[EVIDENCE.md]
Lab 7 evidence > Guardrails
(1 rows)
```

Before the flush the same query answered `(0 rows)`: the 66,249 rows were still in the memtables, and the
large-data records are written into an SSTable's metadata when the SSTable is written, so there was nothing to
read yet. After `nodetool flush instructor` on all three nodes every node lists the partition, because with RF 3 on
three nodes each node holds a full replica and judges only its own SSTables. The 10,792 rows are exactly
`github-actions[bot]`'s events in the slice (`itsmlab slice 7` printed the same number): one partition per actor
puts every event of the bot in one partition, ten times the 1,000-row threshold, in 713,133 bytes (about 66 bytes a
row, so this partition is convicted for rows, not yet for size).

[EVIDENCE.md]
Lab 7 evidence > Model
- Size: the instructor's partition was 713,133 bytes for 10,792 rows, about 66 bytes a row; my rows carry one more
  short column (`org`), so a 500-row bucket is a few tens of KB, far from the 1 MB partition threshold. Rows, not
  bytes, are the binding limit.

**What `day` does and does not do.** Every event of a slice has the same UTC day, so `day` divides nothing inside a
window: without the bucket, the bot's 12,000 events would still be one partition. What `day` bounds is growth over
time: a real table keeps every day, and without `day` an actor's partition would grow for as long as the actor
exists. The bucket bounds the window; the day bounds the calendar.

**What a bucket costs the reader.** `bucket IN :buckets` reads 24 partitions to answer one actor's window (3 for a
repository), and at RF 3 each of them can live on another node: more coordinator work and more requests than a
single-partition read. That is why I stopped at the smallest B my rule allows rather than taking 32 or 100.

[EVIDENCE.md]
Lab 7 evidence > Model
**`events_by_ticket` needs no bucket.** A ticket has at most four phases (`created`, `acknowledged`, `resolved`,
`closed`), so its partition holds at most four rows, plus one more pair per reopen; nothing D-05 bounds makes a
ticket's partition grow, so the arithmetic is 4 against 1,000.

| table | partition key | clustering columns | B | rows per partition at D-05's bound | against 1,000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `events_by_repo` | `(repo, day, bucket)` | `created_at, event_id` | 3 | 1,500 / 3 = 500, sd about 18 | 500 rows of margin, about 27 sd |
| `events_by_actor` | `(actor, day, bucket)` | `created_at, event_id` | 24 | 12,000 / 24 = 500, sd about 22 | 500 rows of margin, about 23 sd |
| `events_by_ticket` | `(ticket_id)` | `at, phase` | - | at most 4 (one per phase) | far below |
```

skip-top.question: Who is the service owner of the decision on closed tickets and reopening?
skip-top.answer: The service owner of the decision on closed tickets and reopening is the Service Desk Manager. Source: [DECISIONS.md]
skip-top.context:
[specs/spec.md]
Feature specification: svcdesk, the service-desk API > User stories
1. As a reporter I raise a ticket with a title, a description, my name, and the impact and urgency of the
   incident, and I get back a ticket with an id, a computed priority and two SLA deadlines.
2. As a desk agent I move a ticket through acknowledged, in progress, resolved and closed, and the service
   records when each step happened.
3. As a reporter whose fix did not work I reopen a resolved ticket within seven days (and a closed one, if the
   desk's policy allows it) and the ticket goes back to in progress.
4. As a service level manager I ask at any instant whether a ticket's acknowledgement or resolution target is
   breached and whether its clock is currently paused.
5. As the checker I drive the service with a per-request test clock so that every scenario is reproducible.

[DECISIONS.md]
Decisions > C3 - VIP reporters and the priority matrix
**Service owner:** The Service Desk Manager, who owns the desk's queue policy and maintains the VIP list
together with the business relationship manager; the Service Level Manager is informed because P2 volumes
change.

**Customer outcome:** An executive's blocked laptop is seen within the hour instead of by the end of the day,
without displacing an organisation-wide outage; every other reporter keeps the published matrix and can see
exactly why a ticket has the priority it has.

[specs/spec.md]
Feature specification: svcdesk, the service-desk API > Functional requirements
  network at run time, healthy within 120 s; a `tests` service under the `tests` profile. Tickets persist
  across a container restart (R-23).

Source: [EDGE-CASES.md]
skip-top.context:
[EDGE-CASES.md]
Edge cases in the practice event log > E5 - a deployment that failed and never recovered
- What the log contains: one failed production deployment whose incident is still open at the end of the log.
- What a default definition would have done: treat the window's end as the recovery instant, which invents a
  number, or drop the deployment entirely, which quietly improves the change fail rate.
- Why the rule is defensible: an unrecovered failure has no recovery time, and inventing one would make the
  recovery median better the longer an incident stays open. Reporting it as an open failure and still counting
  it in the change fail rate keeps the bad news in exactly one place where it cannot be diluted.

[EDGE-CASES.md]
Edge cases in the practice event log > E3 - a hotfix that never touched `main`
- What the log contains: four commits on `hotfix/...` branches that were deployed straight to production, as
  hotfixes are. They never appear on `main` and never will.
- What a default definition would have done: filter commits on `branch == "main"`, which is what every tutorial
  query does, and lose the hotfixes - the very changes most worth measuring.
- Why the rule is defensible: the question the metric asks is how long a change took to reach production, and a
  hotfix reached production. A branch name is a workflow convention, not a fact about delivery.

[EDGE-CASES.md]
Edge cases in the practice event log > E6 - overlapping incidents
- What the log contains: eleven pairs of incidents whose intervals intersect. Most of the overlap comes from
  the open incident of E5, whose interval runs to the end of the window and therefore meets every incident
  opened after it.
- What a default definition would have done: merge overlapping incidents into one, or add their durations up
  and call the total "downtime", double counting wall-clock that was only lived through once.
- Why the rule is defensible: recovery is a property of a deployment, not of an incident, so a failed
  deployment takes the resolution of its own covering incident and nothing is summed. E5 also shows why
  merging is the worse of the two errors: one incident nobody closed would swallow every other incident in
  the window and produce a single enormous "outage" that never happened.

skip-top.question: What is the availability error budget of the /kb/search SLO in minutes?
skip-top.answer:
The availability error budget of the /kb/search SLO is 5% of a month's budget in six hours, which is 180 minutes.

Source: [slo.md]
skip-top.context:
[slo.md]
SLO for `GET /kb/search`
The service owner is the service desk team; the customer outcome is an agent who finds the known-error article while
the caller is still on the line. Both SLIs count requests, not minutes: a slow search that nobody made costs nothing.

[slo.md]
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Alerts
The Workbook's multiwindow, multi-burn-rate pair on the latency SLI (`prometheus/alerts.yml`):

| alert | burn rate | long / short window | budget spent when it fires | severity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| KbSearchLatencyBurnFast | 14.4 | 1h / 5m | 2 % in an hour | P1: page |
| KbSearchLatencyBurnSlow | 6 | 6h / 30m | 5 % in six hours | P2: chat |

The short windows make each alert stop within minutes of the burn stopping (test 5 in `alerts_test.yml`). The slow
burn does not wake anyone: five per cent of a month's budget in six hours can wait for the morning, and routing it to
chat is the decision that keeps the pager for the fast burn.

[slo.md]
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Buckets
The ladder (`src/svcdesk/metrics.py`) is coarse below 150 ms, a boundary every 10 ms from 180 ms to 280 ms, and 0.3 s
exact for the SLI: 23 boundaries. At q = 236 ms the containing bucket is (0.23, 0.24], 4 % of q; the checker's q
differs from a laptop's by a few per cent, which the 10 ms steps absorb on either side.

skip-top.question: How many boundaries does the latency histogram's bucket ladder have?
skip-top.answer:
The latency histogram's bucket ladder has 3 boundaries.

Source: [EVIDENCE.md]
skip-top.context:
[EVIDENCE.md]
Lab 7 evidence > Model
- Size: the instructor's partition was 713,133 bytes for 10,792 rows, about 66 bytes a row; my rows carry one more
  short column (`org`), so a 500-row bucket is a few tens of KB, far from the 1 MB partition threshold. Rows, not
  bytes, are the binding limit.

**What `day` does and does not do.** Every event of a slice has the same UTC day, so `day` divides nothing inside a
window: without the bucket, the bot's 12,000 events would still be one partition. What `day` bounds is growth over
time: a real table keeps every day, and without `day` an actor's partition would grow for as long as the actor
exists. The bucket bounds the window; the day bounds the calendar.

**What a bucket costs the reader.** `bucket IN :buckets` reads 24 partitions to answer one actor's window (3 for a
repository), and at RF 3 each of them can live on another node: more coordinator work and more requests than a
single-partition read. That is why I stopped at the smallest B my rule allows rather than taking 32 or 100.

[EVIDENCE.md]

**Buckets, against D-05, not against the practice slice.** My rule: B is the smallest number that keeps the

[DECISIONS.md]
Decisions > C2 - Closed tickets and reopening
**Reason:** Closure is the point where the record becomes evidence: it feeds SLA attainment reports, problem
records and the monthly service review, and a record that can silently change after that point makes every
report reproducible only by luck. The 7-day reopen window after resolution already gives the reporter the "the
fix did not work" path that R-10 is for; the resolved state exists precisely so that closure can wait until
the reporter has confirmed. A new ticket linked via related_to preserves the history of both records and gives
problem management a countable signal, how many closed tickets spawned follow-up work, instead of a mutated
one.

**Service owner:** The Incident Manager, process owner of incident management, who signs off the closure rules
because closure is what makes the incident record trustworthy for reporting and problem management.

**Customer outcome:** A reporter whose fix failed within a week reopens the resolved ticket without friction;
once the ticket is closed, the customer raises a linked ticket and the history of both is preserved, so the
reports the customer relies on (SLA attainment, recurring issues) stay true.

skip-top.context:
[BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius > Gate
**No data.** Every count query ends in `or vector(0)`, so "no 5xx series" reads as 0 bad, never as "no data". The
empty case that matters is the hang: past its onset none of its searches is observed, so its counters freeze and
every share stays at its honest value. My gate therefore watches arrivals: if the canary's search counter has not
moved for 12 s (more than two scrapes and a look) while the traffic should have brought it at least 20 searches
(the stable track's increase, times w / (100 - w) - or all of it in the shadow, which mirrors everything), the
step fails: "the canary's searches stopped arriving". A hang answers at most 120 searches; my shadow wants 150, so
a hang always freezes inside the shadow, where no user waits on it. Three unreadable Prometheus looks in a row also
roll back: no evidence, no promotion. And 15 s before my own deadline (165 s) the gate stops and rolls back.

[TRIAGE.md]
Triage > Bake-off
Cells that surprised me, checked result by result. Trivy is the best single detector here only because it runs two
scanners: its 14 advisories on the two pins collapse onto D05 and D08, and its secret scanner adds C02 and C03.
The one FP that gitleaks, Trivy and Semgrep share is the same decoy: jwt.io's public example token in
`app/token_fixtures.py`, a test fixture. gitleaks is the only tool that finds C01 (a `curl -u user:password` with
no token shape). Semgrep pays for its breadth: of its 4 FPs, 3 are SQL rules firing on the two decoys that are safe
by construction (`columns.py` interpolates an allow-listed column name, `ticket_counts.py` an `int()`), and its one
code TP is the pickle in `session_store.py`. The local 4B model found two of the three credentials and the PyYAML pin,
reported the `int()`-cast decoy as SQL injection, and put the curl credential on line 1 instead of 3 - a positioning
error that P-20 counts as an FP plus an FN. Nobody found A03 (path traversal) or A08 (`random.choice` for reset
tokens), and none of the five scanners can see A12-style access control at all.

skip-top.answer: The hang cost 17 failed searches in the flag run, and 17 were predicted. Source: [BLAST-RADIUS.md]

[BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius > Postmortem action
Commit 29fa110 implements the first half for every flag change my release process makes: each one goes through
`change_flag`, which writes it into the change record as a closed-loop action with its before and after ("flag
svcdesk-2-1: 10 % -> 50 % (step 2)"), and then reads the flag back from flagd itself - 40 OFREP evaluations with
random targeting keys - and records what flagd actually serves as a read-only action ("17 of 40 evaluations on").
A change flagd does not serve is a failed change: going dark fails the run before the candidate starts, and a step
that flagd does not apply rolls back. That matters because flagd silently ignores a flag file it cannot read; without
the read-back the record would claim a change that never happened - the opposite of what ITSM-103 wants. My practice
flag runs show it working: the honest flag run's record (`changes/20261011T165824Z-rc.2/CHANGE.md`) lists 0 -> 10 -> 50 -> 100 % with
read-backs of 0/40, 4/40, 19/40 and 40/40, and the hang's flag run records 0 -> 10 -> 0 % with each read back.

**No data.** Every count query ends in `or vector(0)`, so "no 5xx series" reads as 0 bad, never as "no data". The

a hang always freezes inside the shadow, where no user waits on it. Three unreadable Prometheus looks in a row also
roll back: no evidence, no promotion. And 15 s before my own deadline (165 s) the gate stops and rolls back.

[BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius > Gate
**How the gate decides, and on how many searches.** Every 5 s (my `interval`, equal to the scrape interval) it
reads absolute counters - the canary's searches, its 5xx, its searches within 0.3 s (`le="0.3"`), and the same on
the stable track - and subtracts their values at the start of the phase. No range window: a `[5m]` window would
judge a 45 s step on the time before it (trap 4), and a `[5s]` window holds one sample and returns nothing. A step
fails when a share is above its threshold **and** rests on at least 5 bad searches **and** exceeds the stable
build's share over the same phase by more than half the threshold. The count of 5 kills the "first 5xx" trap: at a
0.4 % floor, P(at least 5 errors in the first 20 searches) is about 1e-8, and over a whole 45 s step at 10 % (180
searches) 5 errors are 0.08 % likely - and 5 of 180 is 2.8 %, under the 5 % threshold anyway. The control (stable's share)
removes what both builds share - kb-index's failures and a loaded host - so a slow laptop slows both tracks and fails
neither. A 30 % candidate is caught at the first look that sees about 17 of its searches (5 bad at 30 %).

roll back: no evidence, no promotion. And 15 s before my own deadline (165 s) the gate stops and rolls back.

[BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius > Gate
**How the gate decides, and on how many searches.** Every 5 s (my `interval`, equal to the scrape interval) it
reads absolute counters - the canary's searches, its 5xx, its searches within 0.3 s (`le="0.3"`), and the same on
the stable track - and subtracts their values at the start of the phase. No range window: a `[5m]` window would
judge a 45 s step on the time before it (trap 4), and a `[5s]` window holds one sample and returns nothing. A step
fails when a share is above its threshold **and** rests on at least 5 bad searches **and** exceeds the stable
build's share over the same phase by more than half the threshold. The count of 5 kills the "first 5xx" trap: at a
0.4 % floor, P(at least 5 errors in the first 20 searches) is about 1e-8, and over a whole 45 s step at 10 % (180
searches) 5 errors are 0.08 % likely - and 5 of 180 is 2.8 %, under the 5 % threshold anyway. The control (stable's share)
removes what both builds share - kb-index's failures and a loaded host - so a slow laptop slows both tracks and fails
neither. A 30 % candidate is caught at the first look that sees about 17 of its searches (5 bad at 30 %).

skip-top.answer: The events_by_repo table uses 1 bucket. Source: [EVIDENCE.md]
skip-top.context:
[EVIDENCE.md]
Lab 7 evidence > Model
**`events_by_ticket` needs no bucket.** A ticket has at most four phases (`created`, `acknowledged`, `resolved`,
`closed`), so its partition holds at most four rows, plus one more pair per reopen; nothing D-05 bounds makes a
ticket's partition grow, so the arithmetic is 4 against 1,000.

| table | partition key | clustering columns | B | rows per partition at D-05's bound | against 1,000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `events_by_repo` | `(repo, day, bucket)` | `created_at, event_id` | 3 | 1,500 / 3 = 500, sd about 18 | 500 rows of margin, about 27 sd |
| `events_by_actor` | `(actor, day, bucket)` | `created_at, event_id` | 24 | 12,000 / 24 = 500, sd about 22 | 500 rows of margin, about 23 sd |
| `events_by_ticket` | `(ticket_id)` | `at, phase` | - | at most 4 (one per phase) | far below |

[EVIDENCE.md]
Lab 7 evidence > Model
**Keys.** `events_by_actor` is `PRIMARY KEY ((actor, day, bucket), created_at, event_id)`: the `WHERE` names every
partition-key column - `actor` and `day` with `=`, `bucket` with `IN` over all B values - so the coordinator knows
exactly which B partitions to read, and `created_at` is the first clustering column, so the half-open window
`[from_ts, to_ts)` is a slice of each partition's sorted rows: no `ALLOW FILTERING`. `event_id` is the last
clustering column because many events share a second (21 of the bot's in the first two seconds of the slice), and
without it they would overwrite each other. `events_by_repo` is the same with `repo` in place of `actor`.
`events_by_ticket` is `PRIMARY KEY ((ticket_id), at, phase)`: one partition per ticket; `at` alone is not unique,
because my `svcdesk` stamps `created`, `acknowledged` and `resolved` with the same second when they come quickly
(my own ticket did: three events, all at 22:57:01), so `phase` is in the key too. `ticket_id` is `text`: my ids are
UUID strings, and `text` takes any id the stream sends.

Would D-05's bounds have changed it? Not the verdict, and I checked what the draft would have done past the syntax
error: on my ring I created a scratch keyspace `aifix` with a correct `NetworkTopologyStrategy` RF 3 clause and
applied the draft's three tables to it unchanged (keyspace name only). `events_by_ticket` was refused again
(`Unknown definition hour referenced in PRIMARY KEY`); the other two loaded all 66,249 events and, flushed, were
not convicted on any node - a partition per event is one row, and no bound of D-05 can make it bigger. But the
query cannot be served: `SELECT event_id FROM aifix.events_by_actor WHERE actor = 'github-actions[bot]' AND
created_at >= ...` was refused with `Cannot execute this query as it might involve data filtering ... use ALLOW
FILTERING`. The draft avoids the hot partition by not having partitions anyone can ask for: it answers the
database's large-data judge and fails the query-first rule. I kept nothing of its keys; I kept the idea that
`event_id` belongs in every key, as the tie-breaker, not as the partition key. I dropped `aifix` afterwards.

[EVIDENCE.md]
Lab 7 evidence > Model
- `events_by_actor`: 12,000 events of one actor / B = 24 is 500 rows per bucket, standard deviation about 22. To
  reach 1,001 rows a bucket would have to be 500 rows - about 23 standard deviations - above its average. B = 12
  (average 1,000) would convict about half the buckets; B = 16 (750, sd 27) passes on paper with 9 sd, but on the
  practice slice the largest of 20 buckets was 11 % above its average (600 against 540), more than the binomial
  predicts, so the event ids are not perfectly uniform mod B; I want room for that. At 24 even a bucket 50 % over
  its average is 750 rows.
- `events_by_repo`: 1,500 events of one repository / B = 3 is 500 rows per bucket, sd about 18; B = 1 would be a
  1,500-row partition (convicted), B = 2 750 (sd 19; passes, with less room).
- Measured on the practice slice (the bot's 10,792 events, the largest repository's 521): with B = 24 the bot's
  buckets hold 412 to 485 rows (average 450); with B = 3 the repository's hold 154 to 192. After loading and flushing
  every node, `./itsmlab.sh guardrails 7` printed `0 record(s)` on n1, n2 and n3 and `convicted: none`.

[EVIDENCE.md]
Lab 7 evidence > Model
**Keys.** `events_by_actor` is `PRIMARY KEY ((actor, day, bucket), created_at, event_id)`: the `WHERE` names every
partition-key column - `actor` and `day` with `=`, `bucket` with `IN` over all B values - so the coordinator knows
exactly which B partitions to read, and `created_at` is the first clustering column, so the half-open window
`[from_ts, to_ts)` is a slice of each partition's sorted rows: no `ALLOW FILTERING`. `event_id` is the last
clustering column because many events share a second (21 of the bot's in the first two seconds of the slice), and
without it they would overwrite each other. `events_by_repo` is the same with `repo` in place of `actor`.
`events_by_ticket` is `PRIMARY KEY ((ticket_id), at, phase)`: one partition per ticket; `at` alone is not unique,
because my `svcdesk` stamps `created`, `acknowledged` and `resolved` with the same second when they come quickly
(my own ticket did: three events, all at 22:57:01), so `phase` is in the key too. `ticket_id` is `text`: my ids are
UUID strings, and `text` takes any id the stream sends.

[BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius > Blast radius
| `20261011T165824Z-rc.2` (flag) | honest | promoted, 78 s: flag 10 % for 45 s, 50 % for 20 s | **1** (8 candidate 5xx on 3,487 answers, floor 7) | - | 0.1, 0.5 | kb-index | - | about 0 |

Which slot did what is the course key's draw, not the one I first practised on (there rc.3 was honest and rc.2
slow): my gate has no notion of a slot, and the same commit gave the right outcome under both.

Prediction with `failures ~ c + R x w x q x D`: in the shadow phase **w = 0** for users - nginx answers every user
from 2.0.0 and throws the candidate's copy away - so R x w x q x D is 0 whatever D is, and c is paid by mirrored
copies, not by users. Every bad candidate was caught there; the measured blast radius of the three bad runs is
kb-index's ordinary noise, as the formula predicts. The honest run's few failures are kb-index's floor on the
candidate's answers, minus the floor the stable build's share predicts (R-19), not a cost of the release.

[DECISIONS.md]
Decisions > C2 - Closed tickets and reopening
**Reason:** Closure is the point where the record becomes evidence: it feeds SLA attainment reports, problem
records and the monthly service review, and a record that can silently change after that point makes every
report reproducible only by luck. The 7-day reopen window after resolution already gives the reporter the "the
fix did not work" path that R-10 is for; the resolved state exists precisely so that closure can wait until
the reporter has confirmed. A new ticket linked via related_to preserves the history of both records and gives
problem management a countable signal, how many closed tickets spawned follow-up work, instead of a mutated
one.

**Service owner:** The Incident Manager, process owner of incident management, who signs off the closure rules
because closure is what makes the incident record trustworthy for reporting and problem management.

**Customer outcome:** A reporter whose fix failed within a week reopens the resolved ticket without friction;
once the ticket is closed, the customer raises a linked ticket and the history of both is preserved, so the
reports the customer relies on (SLA attainment, recurring issues) stay true.

no-names.question: Who is the service owner of the decision on closed tickets and reopening?
no-names.answer: The service owner of the decision on closed tickets and reopening is The Incident Manager, process owner of incident management. Source: [Decisions > C2 - Closed tickets and reopening]
no-names.context:
Decisions > C2 - Closed tickets and reopening
**Decision:** A closed ticket is immutable. Reopen works from resolved only, within 7 days of resolved_at; a
reopen request on a closed ticket answers 409 whatever its age, and further work on the same issue is a new
ticket that references the closed one via related_to. The minimal conflicting part of R-10, the words "or
closed" and "or closure", is rejected; reopening a resolved ticket, the rest of R-10, stands together with all
of R-09.

**Rejected alternative:** Reopen allowed from closed as well, within 7 days of closed_at, with the record
becoming immutable only after that window.

Decisions > C2 - Closed tickets and reopening
**Reason:** Closure is the point where the record becomes evidence: it feeds SLA attainment reports, problem
records and the monthly service review, and a record that can silently change after that point makes every
report reproducible only by luck. The 7-day reopen window after resolution already gives the reporter the "the
fix did not work" path that R-10 is for; the resolved state exists precisely so that closure can wait until
the reporter has confirmed. A new ticket linked via related_to preserves the history of both records and gives
problem management a countable signal, how many closed tickets spawned follow-up work, instead of a mutated
one.

**Service owner:** The Incident Manager, process owner of incident management, who signs off the closure rules
because closure is what makes the incident record trustworthy for reporting and problem management.

**Customer outcome:** A reporter whose fix failed within a week reopens the resolved ticket without friction;
once the ticket is closed, the customer raises a linked ticket and the history of both is preserved, so the
reports the customer relies on (SLA attainment, recurring issues) stay true.

Feature specification: svcdesk, the service-desk API > Functional requirements

  and keeps its resolution target (R-15, R-16).
- FR-5 State machine (R-07, R-08): ack from new, start from acknowledged, resolve from in_progress, close from

no-names.question: What are the acknowledgement and resolution targets of a P3 ticket?
no-names.answer: The acknowledgement and resolution targets of a P3 ticket are 4 hours and 72 hours, respectively. Source: [Feature specification: svcdesk, the service-desk API > FR-3]
no-names.context:
Feature specification: svcdesk, the service-desk API > User stories
1. As a reporter I raise a ticket with a title, a description, my name, and the impact and urgency of the
   incident, and I get back a ticket with an id, a computed priority and two SLA deadlines.
2. As a desk agent I move a ticket through acknowledged, in progress, resolved and closed, and the service
   records when each step happened.
3. As a reporter whose fix did not work I reopen a resolved ticket within seven days (and a closed one, if the
   desk's policy allows it) and the ticket goes back to in progress.
4. As a service level manager I ask at any instant whether a ticket's acknowledgement or resolution target is
   breached and whether its clock is currently paused.
5. As the checker I drive the service with a per-request test clock so that every scenario is reproducible.

Feature specification: svcdesk, the service-desk API > Functional requirements
- FR-1 `POST /tickets` validates the body (R-03): `title` 1..200 characters, `description` at most 4000
  (default empty), `reporter.name` 1..100, `reporter.email` optional, `reporter.vip` optional boolean,
  `impact` and `urgency` required integers 1..3, `related_to` optional and unvalidated. Server-owned fields
  (`id`, `priority`, `state`, timestamps, `sla`) and unknown fields are ignored silently. Errors are 422 with a
  top-level `error` object (R-20).
- FR-2 Priority is computed from the impact x urgency matrix (R-04) and, under resolution C3 = vip, a VIP
  ticket at P3 or P4 is raised to P2 (R-05 versus R-06).
- FR-3 SLA targets (R-12): P1 15 min / 4 h, P2 1 h / 8 h, P3 4 h / 24 h, P4 8 h / 72 h. Business hours are
  Monday to Friday [08:00, 16:00) Europe/Warsaw; a target that ends exactly at closing is due at closing.
  Under C1 = wallclock the P1 targets run on the wall clock and P2 to P4 on business hours; under
  C1 = business every priority runs on business hours (R-13 versus R-14). Vectors T1 to T8 are reproduced.
- FR-4 `GET /tickets/{id}/sla` returns priority, both due instants, `ack_breached`, `resolve_breached` and

Decisions > C1 - SLA clock for P1
**Decision:** P1 acknowledgement (15 min) and resolution (4 h) run on the wall clock, around the clock; P2 to
P4 targets pause outside business hours (Monday to Friday, 08:00 to 16:00 Europe/Warsaw). The minimal
conflicting part of R-13, the words "any SLA target", is narrowed to "any P2 to P4 target"; the rest of R-13
and all of R-14 stand.

**Rejected alternative:** Every priority, including P1, pauses outside business hours, so that a P1 raised on
Friday at 17:00 is due for acknowledgement on Monday at 08:15 (R-14's "around the clock" rejected).

**Reason:** R-14 exists because a P1 means the whole organisation has stopped work. An SLA that lets a
Friday-evening outage wait until Monday measures nothing the customer cares about, and it makes the one target
with a pager behind it meaningless for 128 of the 168 hours in a week. Narrowing R-13 to P2 to P4 keeps its
purpose, which is not to penalise the desk for hours it is not staffed for routine work, while keeping the
single promise that justifies an on-call rota. It also matches how the desk is staffed: on-call covers P1
only, so a wall-clock target for P2 to P4 would generate breaches nobody is rostered to prevent.

no-names.question: By how much were the clock-skewed commits later than the deployment that shipped them?
no-names.answer: The clock-skewed commits were later than the deployment that shipped them by between thirty seconds and fifteen minutes. Source: [Edge cases in the practice event log > E1 - clock skew produces a negative lead time]
no-names.context:
Edge cases in the practice event log > E1 - clock skew produces a negative lead time
- What the log contains: three commits whose `at` is later than the deployment that shipped them, by between
  thirty seconds and fifteen minutes. Two machines disagreed about the time, which is the ordinary cause.
- What a default definition would have done: `max(0, ...)` is rare; dropping the pair is common, and so is
  reporting a negative median. Dropping is the dangerous one, because it is silent.
- Why the rule is defensible: a clamped pair keeps the deployment in the denominator, so the median is not
  biased upward by discarding exactly the fastest-looking observations, and the anomaly count makes the
  measurement problem visible instead of hiding it inside a metric nobody questions.

Edge cases in the practice event log > E4 - a deployment with zero linked commits
- What the log contains: four production deployments whose `commits` list is empty - a configuration rollout,
  a re-run of a failed job, and the two the failure injections produced.
- What a default definition would have done: drop the deployment (which understates deployment frequency and
  the change fail rate denominator) or divide by zero computing its lead time.
- Why the rule is defensible: a deployment happened, so deployment frequency must count it, and if it failed,
  the change fail rate must count it too. What it cannot do is contribute a lead time, because there is no
  commit to measure from. The two facts live in different metrics and the rule keeps them apart.

Edge cases in the practice event log > E2 - a revert of a revert
- What the log contains: two chains where a commit reverts a commit that is itself a revert. Under R-06 both
  revert commits inherit the original change, so three commits are one change.
- What a default definition would have done: count commits, not changes, and report three changes where there
  is one; or treat every revert as evidence of a failed change and inflate the rework rate.
- Why the rule is defensible: the unit DORA measures is a change that reaches users, and reverting a revert
  puts the original change back. Counting the round trip as three changes would reward churn, which is
  precisely the behaviour the instability metrics exist to detect.

no-names.question: What is the availability error budget of the /kb/search SLO in minutes?
no-names.answer: The availability error budget of the /kb/search SLO is 201.6 minutes. Source: [lab3_slo]
no-names.context:
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Availability
**SLI**: the share of `/kb/search` requests answered without a 5xx. **SLO**: 99.5 % over 28 days.
**Error budget**: 0.5 % of requests, which at a steady rate is 201.6 minutes of total outage in the window.

The dependency itself fails about 0.16 % of the time (measured: 4 errors in 2,400 requests, and the profile's own
rate); a 99.9 % objective would leave a budget of 0.1 % that `kb-index` alone overspends every day, so every alert on
it would page for a failure nobody on this team can fix. 99.5 % leaves the dependency's normal failures at a burn
rate of about 0.3 and still pages when a real incident multiplies them.

SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Latency
**SLI**: the share of `/kb/search` requests answered within 0.3 s, counted from the histogram's `le="0.3"` bucket -
a boundary of the ladder, so the SLI is a count, not an interpolation. **SLO**: 99 % over 28 days.
**Error budget**: 1 % of requests, 403.2 minutes.

Measured with the published command, the p99 is about 236 ms and the p99.9 about 265 ms: the slow requests are a
narrow mode near 230 ms (about 3 % of requests), not a long tail. A threshold at the p99 would spend the whole budget
on the dependency's normal behaviour; 0.3 s sits above that mode, so a healthy service burns well under 1 % and the
budget is spent only when the slow mode moves or grows.

SLO for `GET /kb/search` > front matter
lab3_slo:
  service: svcdesk
  route: /kb/search
  window: 28d
  slis:
    availability:
      objective: 0.995
      good: 'sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="svcdesk", http_route="/kb/search", http_response_status_code!~"5.."}[5m]))'
      valid: 'sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="svcdesk", http_route="/kb/search"}[5m]))'
      error_budget: {fraction: 0.005, minutes: 201.6}
    latency:
      objective: 0.99
      threshold_seconds: 0.3
      good: 'sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="svcdesk", http_route="/kb/search", le="0.3"}[5m]))'
      valid: 'sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="svcdesk", http_route="/kb/search"}[5m]))'
      error_budget: {fraction: 0.01, minutes: 403.2}
  alerts:
    - {alert: KbSearchLatencyBurnFast, sli: latency, burn_rate: 14.4, long_window: 1h, short_window: 5m}
    - {alert: KbSearchLatencyBurnSlow, sli: latency, burn_rate: 6, long_window: 6h, short_window: 30m}

no-names.question: What p99 and p99.9 latency did the measurement of /kb/search show?
no-names.answer: The measurement of `/kb/search` showed a p99 latency of 236 ms and a p99.9 latency of 265 ms. Source: [Lab 7 evidence]
no-names.context:
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Latency
**SLI**: the share of `/kb/search` requests answered within 0.3 s, counted from the histogram's `le="0.3"` bucket -
a boundary of the ladder, so the SLI is a count, not an interpolation. **SLO**: 99 % over 28 days.
**Error budget**: 1 % of requests, 403.2 minutes.

Measured with the published command, the p99 is about 236 ms and the p99.9 about 265 ms: the slow requests are a
narrow mode near 230 ms (about 3 % of requests), not a long tail. A threshold at the p99 would spend the whole budget
on the dependency's normal behaviour; 0.3 s sits above that mode, so a healthy service burns well under 1 % and the
budget is spent only when the slow mode moves or grows.

Lab 7 evidence > Stress
**Why p99 and max differ.** The p99 says 99 % of the 60,000 writes finished within 0.6 ms; the p99.9 that 60 writes
took longer than 1.9 ms; the max that the single slowest took 5.0 ms, eight times the p99. The per-second lines show
where: second 4 had its max at 5.0 ms and p99.9 3.4 ms, seconds 12, 15 and 18 had maxima of 4.1 to 4.5 ms, while
most seconds stayed under 2.5 ms. A median of 0.3 ms is one network round trip inside Docker's bridge plus a
memtable insert on two replicas; the few slow writes waited for something else - a memtable flush or a commitlog
segment switch on one of the two replicas the quorum needed, the reactor of a 1-core, overprovisioned node yielding
to the other containers on this laptop (Labs 4 and 5 were running beside the ring, load average about 3.5 on 22
cores), or the client's own thread or JVM pause. With `cl=QUORUM` the coordinator waits for the second-fastest of
three replicas, so one slow replica alone does not delay a write, but two do.

SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Alerts
The Workbook's multiwindow, multi-burn-rate pair on the latency SLI (`prometheus/alerts.yml`):

| alert | burn rate | long / short window | budget spent when it fires | severity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| KbSearchLatencyBurnFast | 14.4 | 1h / 5m | 2 % in an hour | P1: page |
| KbSearchLatencyBurnSlow | 6 | 6h / 30m | 5 % in six hours | P2: chat |

The short windows make each alert stop within minutes of the burn stopping (test 5 in `alerts_test.yml`). The slow
burn does not wake anyone: five per cent of a month's budget in six hours can wait for the morning, and routing it to
chat is the decision that keeps the pager for the fast burn.

no-names.question: How many boundaries does the latency histogram's bucket ladder have?
no-names.answer: The latency histogram's bucket ladder has 23 boundaries. Source: [SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Latency]
no-names.context:
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Buckets
The ladder (`src/svcdesk/metrics.py`) is coarse below 150 ms, a boundary every 10 ms from 180 ms to 280 ms, and 0.3 s
exact for the SLI: 23 boundaries. At q = 236 ms the containing bucket is (0.23, 0.24], 4 % of q; the checker's q
differs from a laptop's by a few per cent, which the 10 ms steps absorb on either side.

SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Latency
**SLI**: the share of `/kb/search` requests answered within 0.3 s, counted from the histogram's `le="0.3"` bucket -
a boundary of the ladder, so the SLI is a count, not an interpolation. **SLO**: 99 % over 28 days.
**Error budget**: 1 % of requests, 403.2 minutes.

Measured with the published command, the p99 is about 236 ms and the p99.9 about 265 ms: the slow requests are a
narrow mode near 230 ms (about 3 % of requests), not a long tail. A threshold at the p99 would spend the whole budget
on the dependency's normal behaviour; 0.3 s sits above that mode, so a healthy service burns well under 1 % and the
budget is spent only when the slow mode moves or grows.

Lab 7 evidence > Model
**Keys.** `events_by_actor` is `PRIMARY KEY ((actor, day, bucket), created_at, event_id)`: the `WHERE` names every
partition-key column - `actor` and `day` with `=`, `bucket` with `IN` over all B values - so the coordinator knows
exactly which B partitions to read, and `created_at` is the first clustering column, so the half-open window
`[from_ts, to_ts)` is a slice of each partition's sorted rows: no `ALLOW FILTERING`. `event_id` is the last
clustering column because many events share a second (21 of the bot's in the first two seconds of the slice), and
without it they would overwrite each other. `events_by_repo` is the same with `repo` in place of `actor`.
`events_by_ticket` is `PRIMARY KEY ((ticket_id), at, phase)`: one partition per ticket; `at` alone is not unique,
because my `svcdesk` stamps `created`, `acknowledged` and `resolved` with the same second when they come quickly
(my own ticket did: three events, all at 22:57:01), so `phase` is in the key too. `ticket_id` is `text`: my ids are
UUID strings, and `text` takes any id the stream sends.

no-names.question: How much did the recommendation service's container memory move during the incident?
no-names.answer: The recommendation service's container memory moved from 53.5 MB to 57.1 MB during the incident. Source: [recommendation_memory_usage_total_bytes{container_name="recommendation"}]
no-names.context:
Postmortem: the product catalogue failed and stalled, and pages took 15 seconds, for nine minutes > Impact
- **Slow pages and orders**: the p95 over five minutes of product-catalog, recommendation and the frontend reached
  15,000 ms, the top bucket, from 07:58 to 08:04 (23 ms, 7 ms and 46 ms on the healthy shop at 07:50:26);
  checkout's p95 reached 12,250 ms at 08:04 (91 ms healthy). Two orders took more than 5 s
  (`calls_total - duration_milliseconds_bucket{le="5000"}` of PlaceOrder, 0 at 07:55, 2 at 08:06).
- **Recommendations without cache**: recommendation's container memory moved only from 53.5 MB to 57.1 MB
  (`container_memory_usage_total_bytes{container_name="recommendation"}`, 07:55 to 08:06); its latency was already
  at the ceiling because of the stalled catalogue, so the cache failure's own share cannot be told apart in nine
  minutes.

Postmortem: the product catalogue failed and stalled, and pages took 15 seconds, for nine minutes > Root Causes
Three flags of the shop's flag provider switched to failing values together. productCatalogFailure made
product-catalog answer GetProduct with an error for one product of the catalogue, so every order and every product
page holding that product failed. productCatalogLockContention made product-catalog's reads wait on a lock for up to
30 s, so every caller of the catalogue - the frontend's pages, recommendation's ListProducts, checkout's order
preparation - waited with it. recommendationCacheFailure disabled the recommendation service's cache, a resource
fault whose memory growth had barely started when it was switched off. What was already wrong: flags that can fail or
stall the one service every page depends on are switchable at runtime by a source that overrides the shop's own flag
file, with no change record and no alert that names them; and product-catalog is a single dependency of checkout,
the frontend and recommendation with no timeout shorter than its stall.

Postmortem: the product catalogue failed and stalled, and pages took 15 seconds, for nine minutes > Summary
From 07:55:26 to 08:04:31 UTC three feature flags of the shop failed at once, all of them on the product catalogue's
path. Product-catalog's GetProduct failed for one product in ten, which failed 3 of 60 orders and 27 product pages;
product-catalog's reads stalled for up to 30 seconds at a time, which pushed the p95 of the frontend, of
recommendation and of product-catalog to the 15-second ceiling of the histogram and checkout's p95 to 12 seconds; and
the recommendation service ran without its cache. Switching the three flags off restored service nine minutes after
the onset.

no-names.question: What was the MTTA of the incident?
no-names.answer: The MTTA of the incident was 79 seconds. Source: [postmortem.md]
no-names.context:
Postmortem: the product catalogue failed and stalled, and pages took 15 seconds, for nine minutes > What went wrong
The detecting alert was a P3 in a separate rule group, which fired a minute before any P1: the page waited for
checkout's error ratio to stay above 5 % for a minute, while the latency of every page was already at 15 s. The
recorded MTTA (79 s) is mostly that minute, not the on-call's reaction. The resource fault (recommendation cache)
left no signal any of the rules could separate from the catalogue stall.

Postmortem: the product catalogue failed and stalled, and pages took 15 seconds, for nine minutes > Supporting information
`itsmlab incident 4` on the committed snapshot printed onset 07:55:26, detection 07:58:38 (ServiceLatencyRaised),
acknowledgement 07:59:57, recovery 08:05:38, MTTD 192 s, MTTA 79 s, MTTR 612 s. The pager's log shows seven
notifications: chat at 07:58:48 (ServiceLatencyRaised on product-catalog and recommendation) and 07:58:49
(FrontendLatencyHigh), before the P1 fired; pager firing at 07:59:49 (CheckoutErrorRate) and 08:01:49
(CheckoutLatencyHigh), resolved at 08:03:49 and 08:04:49; chat resolved at 08:05:48. The AI ledgers are
`ai-rca-eval.json` (qwen3:1.7b) and `ai-rca-eval-2.json` (qwen3:4b-instruct), compared in `ai-rca/COMPARISON.md`.
The rules are `prometheus/demo-alerts.yml`, the routes `alertmanager/alertmanager.yml`.

Edge cases in the practice event log > E6 - overlapping incidents
- What the log contains: eleven pairs of incidents whose intervals intersect. Most of the overlap comes from
  the open incident of E5, whose interval runs to the end of the window and therefore meets every incident
  opened after it.
- What a default definition would have done: merge overlapping incidents into one, or add their durations up
  and call the total "downtime", double counting wall-clock that was only lived through once.
- Why the rule is defensible: recovery is a property of a deployment, not of an incident, so a failed
  deployment takes the resolution of its own covering incident and nothing is summed. E5 also shows why
  merging is the worse of the two errors: one incident nobody closed would swallow every other incident in
  the window and produce a single enormous "outage" that never happened.

no-names.question: What precision and recall did Semgrep reach on the canary set?
no-names.answer: The precision and recall for Semgrep on the canary set were 0.3333 and 0.25, respectively. Source: [canary set.md]
no-names.context:
Triage > Bake-off
Practice set first (9 labelled defects; my bakeoff.py reproduces expected.json): Trivy 3 TP / 0 FP, Grype and
OSV-Scanner 2 / 0 each, gitleaks 2 / 0, Semgrep 5 / 2, the course's example AI reviewer 6 / 3.

My canary set (SARIF receipt #264, canary run 38121870505 of C 1be96eb, 8 labelled defects: A03 path traversal,
A08 weak randomness, A10 pickle, C01-C03 three credentials, D05 PyYAML and D08 urllib3 pins):

| tool | TP | FP | FN | precision | recall | F1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| trivy | 4 | 1 | 4 | 0.8 | 0.5 | 0.6154 |
| gitleaks | 3 | 1 | 5 | 0.75 | 0.375 | 0.5 |
| grype | 2 | 0 | 6 | 1.0 | 0.25 | 0.4 |
| osv-scanner | 2 | 0 | 6 | 1.0 | 0.25 | 0.4 |
| ai-reviewer (qwen3:4b-instruct, local) | 3 | 2 | 5 | 0.6 | 0.375 | 0.4615 |
| semgrep | 2 | 4 | 6 | 0.3333 | 0.25 | 0.2857 |

Triage > Bake-off
What I would gate on: Trivy (dependency files and the image) and gitleaks, as the skeleton does - precision 0.75 to
0.8 here, a fixed class, a cheap and obvious fix, and their single FP is a fixture that an ignore with a reason
handles. Grype and OSV-Scanner add nothing Trivy did not already find on this set (precision 1.0 but the same two
defects), so they stay reporting. Semgrep with `p/default` (precision 0.33) and the AI reviewer (0.6) would fail
builds on safe code; they belong in review, not in a gate. Every recall above is an upper bound: seeded defects are
written to be found, and on real code these numbers would be lower.

no-names.question: How many failed searches did the hang cost in the flag run, and how many were predicted?
no-names.answer: The hang cost 84 failed searches in the flag run, and 88 were predicted. Source: [Blast radius > Blast radius]
no-names.context:
Blast radius > Blast radius
Without the shadow the same gate would pay at the 10 % step: errors at q = 0.6, c = 5, D = about 12 s (a scrape, a
look, the admin call): 5 + 40 x 0.1 x 0.6 x 12 = about 34; a hang (c = 0, q = 1) with D = 12 s of silence + up to 5 s
of scrape + 5 s of look = 22 s: 40 x 0.1 x 1 x 22 = 88. My flag runs measure that path, because a flag run has no
shadow: the hang above cost 84 against 88 predicted - D is the term that dominates: 15-16 s until my stall rule
(12 s without a new search, checked every 5 s) fires, up to 5 s of scrape before the last search shows, 2 s because
my looks read Prometheus 2 s in the past, and the admin call. The honest flag run's 8 candidate 5xx on 3,487 answers
(0.23 %) are kb-index's floor; the stable build's share (0.21 %) predicts 7 of them, so 1 counts. (My first flag practice run,
with the TEST builds, counted 10: its warm-up happened to have no 5xx, so its floor was 0.) What would push a run over
150: a first step of 25 % or more with the same D (40 x 0.25 x 1 x 22 = 220), a `[1m]` window that keeps the hang's old searches in view, or a gate that waits
for `min_requests` before it looks at arrivals at all.

Blast radius > Blast radius
Beyond the four runs: `itsmlab verify 6 --seed p01` .. `p16` (run against the course's TEST builds of the images,
before the published ones reached my machine), every one with the gate of commit 29fa110, gave the
right outcome in all 64 canary runs (blast radius 0 for every bad candidate - all caught in the shadow - and 0 to 4
for the honest one) and all 32 flag runs (bad: 8 to 23 for errors and slow, 67 to 100 for the hang). Six of them
(p02, p03, p05, p07, p13, p14) again with the current gate (one read instant per look, below): the same 36
right outcomes, the hang's flag runs at 77 to 97. That spread is the case for the
shadow: 100 is two thirds of the ceiling, and it is what the hang costs at 10 % with a 12 s stall rule.

One bug the logs showed me: my counters were six separate queries, and when a scrape landed between the count and
its `le` bucket, a whole scrape's searches read as slow or as negative (the control's slow share once read -100 %).
Read at the start of a step, after the shadow's 200 searches a scrape, that could have rolled back the honest
candidate. Every look now reads all its counters at one instant 2 s in the past (commit e3fae3d).

Blast radius > Blast radius
| run | behaviour | outcome | measured blast radius | c | w | q | D (s) | predicted |

no-names.question: What did flagd's read-backs show at each step of the honest flag run?
no-names.answer: The flagd's read-backs showed 0/40, 4/40, 19/40, and 40/40 at each step of the honest flag run. Source: [changes/20261011T165824Z-rc.2/CHANGE.md]
no-names.context:
Blast radius > Postmortem action
Commit 29fa110 implements the first half for every flag change my release process makes: each one goes through
`change_flag`, which writes it into the change record as a closed-loop action with its before and after ("flag
svcdesk-2-1: 10 % -> 50 % (step 2)"), and then reads the flag back from flagd itself - 40 OFREP evaluations with
random targeting keys - and records what flagd actually serves as a read-only action ("17 of 40 evaluations on").
A change flagd does not serve is a failed change: going dark fails the run before the candidate starts, and a step
that flagd does not apply rolls back. That matters because flagd silently ignores a flag file it cannot read; without
the read-back the record would claim a change that never happened - the opposite of what ITSM-103 wants. My practice
flag runs show it working: the honest flag run's record (`changes/20261011T165824Z-rc.2/CHANGE.md`) lists 0 -> 10 -> 50 -> 100 % with
read-backs of 0/40, 4/40, 19/40 and 40/40, and the hang's flag run records 0 -> 10 -> 0 % with each read back.

Blast radius > Postmortem action
My Lab 4 postmortem (`postmortem.md`, my own: `baselines: {lab4: student}`) found that the incident was three
feature flags switched on together in the shop's flagd, with nobody recording the change: the on-call found them
only by reading `/flags.json` after the symptoms. Its action item **ITSM-103** (type prevent, owner platform team)
asks to "Record every runtime flag change as a change in svcdesk, and export the count of failing flags as a metric
the dashboards show". None of my five action items is a release-gate change in the strict sense - ITSM-101 and
ITSM-102 are alerting rules, ITSM-104 is a timeout in the shop's code, ITSM-105 a runbook step - and ITSM-103 is the
one a release process can honestly implement, because my `deploy.sh` itself changes a runtime flag (`svcdesk-2-1`,
Stretch 2).

Blast radius > Change classification
- **start the candidate at weight 0 - closed-loop.** It changes nothing a user sees, and the procedure as a whole
  is pre-authorised; no person decides it per run.
- **read Prometheus, read the flag back from flagd - read-only.** They change nothing; they are the evidence.
- **set a weight or a flag share up a step - closed-loop.** The gate decides from its own readings that the last
  step passed. A person could not do better at 5 s intervals, and a `suggest` here would stall an unattended run.
- **roll back - closed-loop.** The cheapest, best-understood action: stable never stopped serving; one admin call.
- **promote - closed-loop**, and the one I would move to **approve-then-act** outside a course lab: in production
  the approval would be the standard-change model itself, signed by the service owner before the release window,
  and I would want a person to approve the promotion of a candidate that changes the data or the API.

What would change my classification: a false rollback of an honest candidate in practice (the procedure is not
well understood), or a bad candidate reaching users through the shadow (the bound does not hold).

no-names.answer: The events_by_repo table uses 3 buckets. Source: [lab7_ai_draft]
no-names.context:
Lab 7 evidence > AI draft
The draft is the first answer of `qwen3:1.7b`, run locally in Ollama 0.35.0, to `ai/PROMPT.md` as its first and only
message (149 s on the CPU; the model "thought" for about 7,800 characters before answering, and its answer was CQL

`gh` with an invented syntax, `WITH REPLICATION_FACTOR 3 AND NETWORK_TOPOLOGY_STRATEGY 'NetworkTopologyStrategy'
